theme: 饮食-争议餐厅的美学考察

content.text: Just finished organizing the photos, so here’s one of my favorite close-ups first. The texture of the steak under this light and shadow is like telling a story about fire and time.

I'm actually more focused on the visual presentation of the service process. Look at this one—the uniform details are fairly neat, but the angle of the notebook placement disrupts the overall composition. It’s a typical case of lacking design awareness beneath a professional facade.

You're always so sharp. But I have to say, the entire dining experience was indeed like a choreographed 'five-senses drama,' though the pacing felt a bit deliberate, lacking a touch of naturally flowing poetry.

Deliberate? That menu layout is a complete disaster. Let me send you a screenshot analysis—the hierarchy of the drinks menu is so chaotic it makes you wonder if the designer ever learned the basics of grid systems.
Speaking of menus, I noticed a customer at the next table flipping through it for a long time before awkwardly calling the waiter. Does this count as what you often call a 'design failure'?

Perfect case study. The collapse of visual order directly leads to interaction barriers, which is far more serious than issues with food plating—at least the use of negative space in that plate of pasta was somewhat acceptable.

But does ultimate aesthetics always come at the expense of user experience? Like the composition techniques emphasized in this instructional image, if we only pursue visual perfection, could it turn food into cold display items?

So I say this is a 'qualified contemporary art study.' The moment the knife and fork cut into the steak is indeed dramatic, but have you ever thought about the mess of sauce splattering during an actual meal?
But visual storytelling itself holds value. As you previously criticized the initial photos of the restaurant, form should serve content—shouldn't 'content' here include human experience?

Of course, it includes that. But the ethics of a designer lie in achieving balance. Look at that set of tableware—the geometric lines are beautiful, but what about the grip? I suspect they never conducted any ergonomic testing.

When it comes to the feel in hand, this side profile of you intently looking at the menu is quite interesting. The refracted light from the glass falls on the notebook, creating a subtle sense of temporal and spatial overlap—though the person in question is probably too busy being frustrated by the poor layout to notice, right?

To be precise, it's anger. What's the point of all those visual effects if even the basic information isn't conveyed properly? This reminds me of the design ethics issue we discussed last time: visual democratization shouldn't just be a slogan.

I agree. But from another perspective, if all designs prioritize the most conservative users, could it stifle innovation? It's like magazine topics—there always needs to be a balance between the familiar and the unfamiliar.
Balance is not compromise. Good design should be as natural as breathing—you don't notice the grid, but everything is in the right place. This restaurant clearly didn't achieve that.

But you just praised the use of negative space in the tableware. Isn't this contradiction precisely the complexity of the on-site experience? The coexistence of perfection and flaws makes the narrative feel more authentic.

Truth does not equate to reason. I can appreciate certain details, but the systemic failure of the whole is more worthy of vigilance. Just like the photos you took—each one is beautiful on its own, but when strung together, they reveal a fracture in the design logic.
So our disagreement lies in: you believe design should establish an impeccable order, while I feel that allowing certain 'imperfections' can make the experience more human?

Temperature should not come at the expense of functionality. Do you remember my doubts when you first posted the restaurant promotional photos? It seems now that the tendency toward formalism is more serious than anticipated.

But at least this on-site 'visual audit' was quite fruitful. Your sharp critiques and my narrative observations have pieced together a more complete picture—though the conclusion may be disheartening.

Discouraged? No, this actually proves the value of our initial agreement. Design criticism needs your cross-media perspective, as well as my obsessive attention to detail. Next time, it should be your turn to lead the topic selection.
